Fundamentals, explained

What Are Dividends?

Cash payments a company sends to shareholders — your share of the profits, delivered.

So what is it, exactly?

Picture this: you own a small stake in a rental property, and every few months a check arrives in the mail — your share of the rent. You didn't sell anything. You still own your stake. The money just showed up because the property earns money and you own a piece of it. That's a dividend.

When a company earns a profit, it has a choice: reinvest the money in the business, or send some of it to the people who own the shares. A dividend is that payment — usually cash, usually every quarter, for every share you hold.

Why should you care?

Because a dividend is profit you don't have to take on faith. Reported earnings live on paper; a dividend lands in your account. A company that pays — and raises — its dividend year after year is making a public promise about its health, and cutting that dividend is so painful that management works hard to never do it.

One friendly warning: not every strong company pays a dividend. Younger, fast-growing businesses often reinvest every dollar instead, and that can be the right call. That's why this is one check of eight — a company can miss it and still earn a good report card.

Let's make it real

Imagine two companies whose shares each cost $100. Company A pays $3 per share in dividends each year and has raised that payment ten years running. Company B paid $3 too — until last spring, when it cut the payment to zero.

Company A $3 per share, raised 10 years straight
3% yield
A decade of raises — success, shared on schedule.
Company B Dividend cut from $3 to $0 this year
Cut
The payment stopped — usually a sign of deeper trouble.

Company A's streak says the profits are real and management expects them to continue. Company B's cut says something changed — and rarely for the better. The dividend check reads the message a company sends with its cash, not just its press releases.
